bill.title: To extend the Secure Rural Schools and Community Self-Determination Act of 2000.
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the Subcommittee on Forestry and Horticulture.
bill.officialSummary: This bill extends and modifies the Secure Rural Schools and Community Self-Determination Act of 2000, including by extending payments made to states and counties containing federal land through FY2026, providing for payments for FY2024 and FY2025, extending the authority of counties to initiate projects using such funds through FY2028, and extending the authority to initiate projects proposed by resource advisory committees through FY2028.

classification.plainSummary: This bill extends a program that makes payments to states and counties that contain federal land. It would continue these payments through fiscal year 2026 and provide specific payments for 2024 and 2025. The bill also extends the authority for counties and local advisory committees to use these funds for projects through 2028.

industries.rationale: The bill provides direct payments to state and county governments containing federal land and governs how they may spend those funds.
Timber harvesting and resource extraction on federal lands directly affect funding formulas under this rural schools program.
The Secure Rural Schools program historically directs a portion of payments to support schools in counties with federal land.

plain.whatItDoes: This bill would extend and change the Secure Rural Schools and Community Self-Determination Act of 2000, including by extending payments made to states and counties containing federal land through the 2026 budget year, providing for payments for the 2024 budget year and 2025, extending the authority of counties to initiate projects using such funds through the 2028 budget year, and extending the authority to initiate projects proposed by resource advisory committees through the 2028 budget year.
plain.whoItTouches: People who use public land, and people who live beside it.
plain.everydayEffect: If it passed, the change would show up in what may be done on that land. Nothing has changed yet. Most bills never become law.
plain.source: Reworded from the official summary. Staff at the Congressional Research Service wrote that summary. It is public domain, and the full text of it is further down this page.

method.formula: score = Σ_industries ( donorShare(industry) × billWeight(industry) ), where billWeight = classifierConfidence / Σ classifierConfidence. Range 0–1, read as a weighted share of disclosed itemized money.

ordinary.text: They wrote this bill. Sponsoring a bill about your own district's industry is the ordinary case, not the odd one.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
